NG-AB.title: God's Own State
NG-AB.note: Abia's nickname reflects its strong Christian religious identity and its role as a commercial engine of the southeast.

NG-AB.title: Aba's manufacturing fame
NG-AB.note: Aba, Abia's commercial capital, is nationally known for locally manufactured shoes, bags, and garments branded 'Aba-made.'

NG-AB.title: Arochukwu and the Long Juju
NG-AB.note: Arochukwu was historically home to the powerful Aro Confederacy and the Ibini Ukpabi oracle ('Long Juju'), central to pre-colonial trade and slave-trade networks in the region.

NG-AB.title: Ohafia war dance (Ikpirikpe-Ogu)
NG-AB.note: Ohafia is known for its warrior tradition, expressed in the Ikpirikpe-Ogu war dance.

NG-AB.title: National War Museum, Umuahia
NG-AB.note: Umuahia holds a museum of the 1967-70 civil war and served as an administrative seat of Biafra after Enugu fell.

NG-AD.title: Fombina origins
NG-AD.note: Adamawa takes its name from the historic Adamawa Emirate ('Fombina'), founded in the 1800s and once spanning into present-day Cameroon.

NG-AD.title: Ethnic diversity
NG-AD.note: Adamawa is one of Nigeria's most linguistically diverse states, home to dozens of distinct ethnic groups including Fulani, Bura, Mumuye, and Margi.

NG-AD.title: Sukur Cultural Landscape
NG-AD.note: The Sukur Cultural Landscape in Madagali LGA was inscribed by UNESCO in 1999 as Nigeria's first World Heritage Site, with the Hidi's hilltop palace, terraced fields and iron-working remains.

NG-AD.title: Lamido of Adamawa
NG-AD.note: The Lamido of Adamawa heads the Adamawa Emirate (Fombina) at Yola.

NG-AD.title: Hama Bachama
NG-AD.note: The Hama Bachama is the traditional head of the Bachama (Bwatiye) people.

NG-AK.title: Land of Promise
NG-AK.note: Akwa Ibom's nickname reflects its oil wealth and aspirations for economic promise following its creation from Cross River State in 1987.

NG-AK.title: Ibibio and Annang heartland
NG-AK.note: The state is the traditional homeland of the Ibibio and Annang peoples, known for distinct masquerade and mmanwu traditions.

NG-AK.title: Ekpo masquerade society
NG-AK.note: Ekpo is the ancestral masquerade society of the Ibibio and Annang.

NG-AK.title: Mbopo fattening-room rite
NG-AK.note: Mbopo is the Ibibio rite of passage in which young women were traditionally prepared for marriage in a fattening house.

NG-AN.title: Light of the Nation
NG-AN.note: Anambra's nickname nods to its historic role in Nigeria's commercial and intellectual life, particularly through Onitsha and Nnewi's trading economies.

NG-AN.title: Igbo-Ukwu bronzes
NG-AN.note: Anambra is the site of the Igbo-Ukwu archaeological finds — sophisticated bronze artefacts dated to the 9th century, among the earliest evidence of advanced metalworking in West Africa.

NG-AN.title: Nnewi's industrial cluster
NG-AN.note: Nnewi has grown into one of Nigeria's leading indigenous auto-parts manufacturing hubs, nicknamed 'the Japan of Africa' by some commentators.

NG-AN.title: Ofala Festival (Onitsha)
NG-AN.note: The Obi of Onitsha's annual emergence from seclusion, held in October and drawing large crowds. Onitsha's festival cycle also includes Umatu (first maize), Owuwa Ji (new yam) and Ifejioku (January).

NG-AN.title: Uzo-iyi Masquerade Festival
NG-AN.note: Umuoji's four-day masquerade festival opens the rainy season in March.

period.note: Four days at the start of the rains

NG-AN.title: Ijele masquerade
NG-AN.note: Ijele is Africa's largest masquerade, inscribed by UNESCO in 2009 and mainly found in Anambra.

NG-AN.title: Eze Nri
NG-AN.note: The Eze Nri holds ritual kingship at Nri, associated with the Nri Kingdom.

NG-BA.title: Pearl of Tourism
NG-BA.note: Bauchi's nickname reflects Yankari National Park, Nigeria's most-visited wildlife reserve, located within the state.

NG-BA.title: Bauchi Emirate
NG-BA.note: Bauchi Emirate was founded in the early 19th century by Yakubu during the Sokoto jihad.

NG-BA.title: Sayawa (Zaar) communities
NG-BA.note: The Sayawa (Zaar) of Tafawa Balewa, Bogoro and Dass are among southern Bauchi's largest non-Hausa groups.

NG-BY.title: Glory of All Lands
NG-BY.note: Bayelsa, created in 1996, is one of Nigeria's newest and most riverine states, almost entirely within the Niger Delta.

NG-BY.title: Birthplace of a president
NG-BY.note: Bayelsa is the home state of Goodluck Jonathan, Nigeria's president from 2010 to 2015, the country's first from a Niger Delta minority background.

NG-BY.title: Oloibiri oil discovery
NG-BY.note: Oloibiri in Ogbia LGA saw Nigeria's first commercial oil discovery in 1956, with production beginning in 1958.

NG-BY.title: Nembe and the Akassa raid
NG-BY.note: Nembe (Brass) was a major palm-oil trading kingdom whose people carried out the 1895 Akassa raid on the Royal Niger Company.

NG-BE.title: Food Basket of the Nation
NG-BE.note: Benue's nickname reflects its role as one of Nigeria's largest producers of yams, soybeans, and citrus.

NG-BE.title: Tiv and Idoma home
NG-BE.note: The state is the traditional home of the Tiv people (one of Nigeria's largest ethnic groups) and the Idoma people, each with distinct language and masquerade traditions.

NG-BE.title: Kwagh-hir
NG-BE.note: Kwagh-hir is Tiv theatre that mixes puppetry, masquerade, music, dance and storytelling, inscribed by UNESCO in 2019.

NG-BE.title: Tor Tiv
NG-BE.note: The Tor Tiv is the paramount ruler of the Tiv, with his palace at Gboko.

NG-BE.title: Eje Alekwu festival
NG-BE.note: Idoma communities honour the ancestral spirit Alekwu in a festival of masquerades, communal hunting and rites before the harvest.

period.note: Late March to early April

NG-BE.title: Och'Idoma
NG-BE.note: The Och'Idoma is the paramount ruler of the Idoma, whose palace at Otukpo is the focus of the Alekwu festival.

NG-BE.title: Ige-Agba new yam festival
NG-BE.note: The Igede of Oju and Obi celebrate the new yam with the Ige-Agba festival.

period.note: First week of September

NG-BO.title: Kanem-Bornu legacy
NG-BO.note: Borno's name descends from the historic Kanem-Bornu Empire, one of Africa's longest-surviving states, dating back over a thousand years.

NG-BO.title: Home of Peace (aspirational)
NG-BO.note: Borno's 'Home of Peace' nickname predates the security challenges of the 2010s-2020s and reflects its historical role as a centre of Islamic scholarship and trans-Saharan trade.

NG-BO.title: Shehu of Borno
NG-BO.note: The Shehu of Borno heads the Borno Emirate, succeeding the ancient Mai of Kanem-Bornu.

NG-BO.title: Mai of Biu
NG-BO.note: The Mai of Biu rules the Bura (Babur) chiefdom of the Biu plateau.

NG-CR.title: The People's Paradise
NG-CR.note: Cross River's nickname points to its rainforest tourism assets — Obudu Mountain Resort, Cross River National Park, and the Calabar Carnival.

NG-CR.title: Calabar Carnival
NG-CR.note: Calabar hosts a December carnival billed as Africa's biggest street party, drawing large domestic and diaspora crowds.

period.note: Runs through the December festive season

NG-CR.title: Old Calabar's Atlantic trade history
NG-CR.note: Calabar was a major Atlantic-era Efik trading port from the 17th century, historically significant in both palm-oil trade and the transatlantic slave trade.

NG-CR.title: Ekpe (Leopard) society
NG-CR.note: Ekpe is the Efik institution of governance and secret society, with branches among the Ibibio and Igbo of neighbouring states.

NG-CR.title: Leboku New Yam Festival
NG-CR.note: The Yakurr (Yako) people mark the new yam with the three-week Leboku, which honours the earth goddess and ancestors and includes a parade of engaged maidens. Its international edition is held at Ugep.

period.note: About mid-August to mid-September

NG-CR.title: Ikom monoliths
NG-CR.note: Hundreds of carved stone monoliths around Ikom and Etung are among the region's best-known archaeological and artistic remains.

NG-DE.title: The Big Heart
NG-DE.note: Delta's nickname reflects both its geography — sitting within the Niger Delta — and a self-styled reputation for hospitality.

NG-DE.title: Multi-ethnic makeup
NG-DE.note: Delta is home to several distinct groups — Urhobo, Igbo (Anioma), Ijaw, Isoko, and Itsekiri — each with its own language and traditional rulership.

NG-DE.title: Amaseikumor Festival
NG-DE.note: The Ijaw of Gbaramatu Kingdom in Warri South West LGA celebrate a seven-day annual festival built around confession, cleansing and the renewal of ancestral covenants.

NG-DE.title: Olu of Warri and coronation anniversary
NG-DE.note: The Olu of Warri heads the Itsekiri Kingdom, seated at Warri, with Ode-Itsekiri as the cradle of the people. His coronation anniversary is marked with a week of events each August.

period.note: Week-long coronation anniversary celebrations

NG-DE.title: Ghigho Aghofen (Palace Watch)
NG-DE.note: The Olu of Warri introduced the Palace Watch ceremony in December 2021, in which an Itsekiri community takes turns keeping watch over the palace.

period.note: First held on 18 December 2021

NG-DE.title: Ogunme
NG-DE.note: A cultural form reported as unique to the Itsekiri people. Details still to be confirmed with local sources.

NG-DE.title: Ekpu (Urhobo ancestral figures)
NG-DE.note: Ekpu are carved ancestral memorial figures of the Urhobo.

NG-DE.title: Asagba of Asaba
NG-DE.note: The Asagba is the traditional ruler of Asaba, capital of Delta State.

NG-EB.title: Salt of the Nation
NG-EB.note: Ebonyi's nickname references Okposi and Uburu, historic centres of local salt-lake production that supplied trade routes across the pre-colonial southeast.

NG-EB.title: Nigeria's youngest Igbo state
NG-EB.note: Ebonyi was created only in 1996, carved from Enugu and Abia States, making it one of the newest Igbo-speaking states.

NG-EB.title: Okumkpa (Afikpo)
NG-EB.note: Okumkpa is a satirical masquerade performance of the Afikpo (Ehugbo) Igbo.

NG-ED.title: Heartbeat of Nigeria
NG-ED.note: Edo's nickname reflects Benin City's historic centrality as one of Africa's oldest and most sophisticated pre-colonial kingdoms.

NG-ED.title: Benin Kingdom heritage
NG-ED.note: The Benin Kingdom's royal court produced the famed Benin Bronzes, many looted by British forces in 1897 and now the subject of ongoing international restitution efforts.

NG-ED.title: Igue Festival
NG-ED.note: Benin's Igue is the annual royal festival of blessing and renewal centred on the Oba's palace.

NG-ED.title: Igun Eronmwon bronze casters' guild
NG-ED.note: The Igun Eronmwon is the hereditary guild of royal bronze casters of Benin City.

NG-ED.title: Onojie of Esan
NG-ED.note: Esan communities are ruled by kings titled Onojie, heading many small kingdoms.

NG-ED.title: Otaru of Auchi
NG-ED.note: The Otaru of Auchi is the leading traditional ruler among the Etsako (Afemai).

NG-EK.title: Land of Honour and Integrity
NG-EK.note: Ekiti's nickname reflects a self-image tied to its historically strong output of professionals, academics, and civil servants relative to its small size.

NG-EK.title: Youngest of the Yoruba states
NG-EK.note: Ekiti was created in 1996, carved from Ondo State, making it one of Nigeria's newest states.

NG-EK.title: Udiroko Festival
NG-EK.note: Ado-Ekiti's annual Udiroko festival gathers the Ewi, chiefs and indigenes at the palace under the big Uroko tree. It is dated to around 1310 AD and is treated as the town's new year.

period.note: Recent editions have fallen in late August

NG-EK.title: Olosunta Festival
NG-EK.note: Ikere-Ekiti honours Olosunta Mountain, a landmark tied to the town's founding, in an annual festival.

NG-EK.title: Ewi of Ado-Ekiti
NG-EK.note: The Ewi is the paramount ruler of Ado-Ekiti; other major Ekiti thrones include the Olukere of Ikere.

NG-EN.title: Coal City State
NG-EN.note: Enugu's nickname comes from the coal deposits discovered in 1909 that turned it into Nigeria's first major coal-mining industrial centre.

NG-EN.title: Biafran wartime capital
NG-EN.note: Enugu briefly served as the capital of the breakaway Republic of Biafra during the early phase of the 1967-70 Nigerian Civil War.

NG-EN.title: Odo Masquerade Festival
NG-EN.note: The Odo festival, in which masks are said to bring the dead back among the living, is held every two years in Ngwo (Udi), Ebe, Ezeagu and parts of Nsukka.

NG-EN.title: Mmanwu Festival
NG-EN.note: The Federal Ministry of Information lists a masquerade festival held in Enugu each November to usher in the new yam.

NG-FC.title: Centre of Unity
NG-FC.note: The Federal Capital Territory's nickname reflects the deliberate choice of a centrally located, ethnically neutral site for Nigeria's capital.

NG-FC.title: A planned capital
NG-FC.note: Abuja was purpose-built starting in 1976 and officially replaced Lagos as Nigeria's federal capital in 1991.

NG-FC.title: Zuma Rock landmark
NG-FC.note: A 725-metre granite monolith just outside the FCT along the Kaduna expressway has become an unofficial national symbol, once featured on the 100-naira note.

NG-FC.title: Abuja International Carnival
NG-FC.note: Abuja stages a national carnival showcasing performances from across Nigeria; the Federal Ministry of Arts, Culture and Creative Economy lists the 2024 edition.

NG-FC.title: Ona of Abaji
NG-FC.note: The Ona of Abaji heads the Abaji Emirate, an Ebira-Koto (Egbura) traditional state in the FCT.

NG-GO.title: Jewel in the Savannah
NG-GO.note: Gombe's nickname reflects its savanna landscape and relatively recent emergence as a state, created in 1996 from Bauchi State.

NG-GO.title: Emirate of Gombe
NG-GO.note: Gombe Emirate was founded in the early 1800s by Buba Yero during the Sokoto jihad.

NG-GO.title: Mai Tangale
NG-GO.note: The Tangale of Billiri and Kaltungo are led by the Mai Tangale, alongside the neighbouring Waja.

NG-IM.title: Eastern Heartland
NG-IM.note: Imo's nickname reflects its central position within Igboland and its historically dense population.

NG-IM.title: Oguta Lake
NG-IM.note: Imo is home to Oguta Lake, one of Nigeria's largest natural lakes and a popular local tourism site.

NG-IM.title: Ikeji Festival (Arondizuogu)
NG-IM.note: Arondizuogu's Ikeji festival celebrates the harvest of the first yams over four Igbo market days (Eke, Orie, Afor and Nkwo), ending with the big masquerades at Nkwo-Achi. The festival is traced to Arochukwu.

NG-IM.title: Ahiajoku Lecture
NG-IM.note: The Ahiajoku Lecture is an annual cultural and intellectual lecture series of the Imo State Government, launched in 1979.

NG-JI.title: The New World
NG-JI.note: Jigawa's nickname reflects its status as one of Nigeria's newest states, carved from Kano State in 1991.

NG-JI.title: Jigawa's emirates
NG-JI.note: Jigawa's historic emirates include Dutse, Hadejia, Gumel, Kazaure and Ringim.

NG-JI.title: Hadejia-Nguru wetlands
NG-JI.note: The Hadejia-Nguru floodplain, a Ramsar-listed wetland shared with Yobe State, supports fishing, farming and migratory birds.

NG-KD.title: Centre of Learning
NG-KD.note: Kaduna's nickname reflects Ahmadu Bello University and a dense concentration of federal colleges and military training institutions.

NG-KD.title: Colonial planned capital
NG-KD.note: Kaduna was founded around 1913 by Frederick Lugard as the administrative capital of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria.

NG-KD.title: Afan National Festival
NG-KD.note: The Afan festival of the Kagoro (Gworok) people is held on 1 January at the Chief of Kagoro's palace in Kaura LGA. It marks the end of the farming season and the start of hunting, and is said to be around 400 years old.

period.note: Held on 1 January

NG-KD.title: Nok terracotta culture
NG-KD.note: The Nok culture, named after Nok village in Jaba LGA, produced West Africa's earliest known large terracotta sculptures more than two thousand years ago.

NG-KD.title: Emir of Zazzau
NG-KD.note: The Emir of Zazzau heads the historic Zazzau emirate, seated at Zaria.

NG-KN.title: Centre of Commerce
NG-KN.note: Kano's nickname reflects its millennium-old role as one of West Africa's most important trans-Saharan trading cities.

NG-KN.title: Kano city walls
NG-KN.note: The old walled city of Kano (Kano birni) was enclosed by defensive mud walls dating to the 15th century, remnants of which still stand today.

NG-KN.title: Most populous state
NG-KN.note: Kano is Nigeria's most populous state, a status tied to its long history as a dense urban trading centre.

NG-KN.title: Sallah Durbar (Hawan Sallah)
NG-KN.note: Mounted horsemen in colourful regalia pay homage to the Emir during the Eid celebrations in Kano, Katsina, Zaria and other northern emirates.

period.note: Follows Eid-el-Fitr and Eid-el-Kabir, so it moves with the Islamic calendar

NG-KN.title: Kano Emirate
NG-KN.note: The Emir of Kano heads one of Nigeria's oldest and most prominent emirates. Its structure has been subject to recent legal and political change, so confirm the current status before publishing.

NG-KN.title: Kofar Mata dye pits
NG-KN.note: The historic indigo dye pits near Kofar Mata are a symbol of Kano's textile tradition and are often dated to the late 15th century.

NG-KT.title: Home of Hospitality
NG-KT.note: Katsina's nickname reflects a long-standing local reputation for hospitality to traders and travellers along historic caravan routes.

NG-KT.title: Hausa Bakwai city-state
NG-KT.note: Katsina was one of the seven original Hausa city-states (Hausa Bakwai) and a major centre of Islamic scholarship before and after the Sokoto Jihad.

NG-KT.title: Daura and the Bayajidda legend
NG-KT.note: Daura is regarded in Hausa tradition as the ancestral home of the Hausa people, linked to the Bayajidda legend.

NG-KE.title: Land of Equity
NG-KE.note: Kebbi's nickname reflects the historic Kebbi Kingdom's reputation for a relatively egalitarian, non-centralised political structure compared to neighbouring emirates.

NG-KE.title: Argungu Fishing Festival
NG-KE.note: Kebbi hosts the Argungu International Fishing and Cultural Festival, one of Nigeria's most famous traditional festivals. Its main event is a bare-hand and net fishing contest on the Matan Fada River, and it was created to mark the end of old hostilities between the Sokoto Caliphate and the Kebbi Kingdom.

period.note: Usually four days; editions have been irregular in recent years

NG-KE.title: Historic emirates of Kebbi
NG-KE.note: Kebbi's historic emirates include Argungu, Gwandu, Yauri and Zuru, each with its own ruler.

NG-KO.title: The Confluence State
NG-KO.note: Kogi's nickname comes from the meeting of the Niger and Benue rivers at Lokoja — Nigeria's two largest rivers converge within the state.

NG-KO.title: Three major groups, one state
NG-KO.note: Unlike many states with one dominant ethnic identity, Kogi is genuinely tri-ethnic: the Igala in the east, the Ebira around Okene, and Okun-Yoruba communities in the west, each with distinct language and traditional rulership.

NG-KO.title: First capital of Northern Nigeria
NG-KO.note: Lokoja was the first capital of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, which Frederick Lugard proclaimed there in 1900, before the seat moved to Zungeru in 1902.

NG-KO.title: Ocho Festival
NG-KO.note: Ocho is an ancient Igala hunting festival at Idah that opens the hunting and farming season. It was banned in 1963 and revived in 2018.

NG-KO.title: Attah Igala
NG-KO.note: The Attah Igala is the paramount ruler of the Igala kingdom, seated at Idah.

NG-KO.title: Echane (Eche-Ane) masquerade festival
NG-KO.note: Ebira communities stage the Echane masquerade festival in rotation from one district to another between April and June. Ebira festivals also include Ekuechi and the Eche-Ori new yam rites at Ihima and Eganyi.

period.note: Rotates between Ebira districts

NG-KO.title: Ohinoyi of Ebiraland
NG-KO.note: The Ohinoyi is the paramount ruler of the Ebira, seated at Okene.

NG-KO.title: Ovie Orese
NG-KO.note: Ovie Orese is a marital rite for young women in Ogori land, listed by the Federal Ministry of Information.

NG-KO.title: Obaro of Kabba
NG-KO.note: The Obaro of Kabba is the leading Okun-Yoruba ruler of western Kogi.

NG-KW.title: State of Harmony
NG-KW.note: Kwara's nickname reflects its position as a cultural bridge between the Yoruba south and Hausa-Fulani north, with a historically peaceful record of coexistence.

NG-KW.title: Ilorin's dual identity
NG-KW.note: Ilorin transitioned from a Yoruba town to a Fulani emirate in the early 19th century after the Sokoto Jihad, giving Kwara's capital a distinctive blended Yoruba-Hausa identity found almost nowhere else in Nigeria.

NG-KW.title: Emir of Ilorin
NG-KW.note: The Emir of Ilorin heads the Ilorin Emirate, founded in the 1820s, which fused Yoruba and Fulani-Hausa traditions.

NG-KW.title: Etsu Patigi
NG-KW.note: The Etsu Patigi is the Nupe ruler of Patigi on the Niger River.

NG-KW.title: Patigi Regatta
NG-KW.note: Patigi hosts a river regatta on the Niger, one of Kwara's best-known cultural events.

NG-LA.title: Centre of Excellence
NG-LA.note: Lagos's nickname reflects its status as Nigeria's commercial and cultural capital, though no longer the political capital since 1991.

NG-LA.title: Former national capital
NG-LA.note: Lagos was Nigeria's federal capital from independence in 1960 until Abuja formally took over in 1991.

NG-LA.title: Africa's most populous city
NG-LA.note: Lagos is widely regarded as Africa's most populous urban agglomeration, with a metropolitan population estimated well above 15 million.

NG-LA.title: Eyo Festival (Adamu Orisha Play)
NG-LA.note: Lagos Island's white-robed Eyo masquerades parade through the streets, traditionally staged to mark the passing of an important Lagosian and for major ceremonial occasions. The main Eyo groups are Adimu, Laba, Oniko, Ologede and Agere.

period.note: Held when occasion demands, not on a fixed date

NG-LA.title: Zangbeto (Egun night guardians)
NG-LA.note: Zangbeto are straw-cloaked spirit figures of the Egun people, believed to guard communities at night and whose spinning dance is a signature performance in Badagry and across the Benin border.

NG-LA.title: Oba of Lagos and the Idejo chiefs
NG-LA.note: The Oba of Lagos rules from the Iga Idunganran palace on Lagos Island alongside the Idejo (White Cap) chiefs, the land-owning chiefly houses of old Eko.

NG-LA.title: Badagry slave-trade heritage
NG-LA.note: Badagry was a major slave-trade port, and its heritage sites include the Point of No Return and historic missionary buildings.

NG-NA.title: Home of Solid Minerals
NG-NA.note: Nasarawa's nickname reflects its deposits of barite, salt, and other solid minerals, alongside its proximity to Abuja.

NG-NA.title: Traditional rulers of Nasarawa
NG-NA.note: Nasarawa's historic thrones include the Aren Eggon, the Osana of Doma and the Emirs of Lafia and Keffi.

NG-NI.title: The Power State
NG-NI.note: Niger's nickname reflects hosting Kainji and Shiroro Dams, two of Nigeria's three major hydroelectric power stations.

NG-NI.title: Nigeria's largest state by area
NG-NI.note: Niger is Nigeria's largest state by land area, spanning over 76,000 sq km.

NG-NI.title: Etsu Nupe
NG-NI.note: The Etsu Nupe is the paramount ruler of the Nupe, seated at Bida.

NG-NI.title: Bida brass and glass-bead craft
NG-NI.note: Bida is known for brasswork and glass-bead making passed down in Nupe craft guilds.

NG-NI.title: Gani festival
NG-NI.note: Bida marks the Prophet's birthday with the Gani festival of parades and Nupe pageantry.

period.note: Moves with the Islamic calendar

NG-NI.title: Emir of Kontagora
NG-NI.note: The Emir of Kontagora holds the historic title Sarkin Sudan.

NG-OG.title: Gateway State
NG-OG.note: Ogun's nickname reflects its position bordering Lagos and Benin Republic, historically a corridor for trade between the coast and the interior.

NG-OG.title: Birthplace of noted leaders
NG-OG.note: Ogun State, particularly Abeokuta, produced several of Nigeria's most prominent 20th-century nationalist and political figures.

NG-OG.title: Olumo Rock
NG-OG.note: The Egba people settled at Abeokuta under Olumo Rock in 1830, using its caves as a wartime refuge; the rock remains the city's defining landmark.

NG-OG.title: Ojude Oba Festival
NG-OG.note: Age-grade groups (Regberegbe) of Ijebu-Ode parade in matching regalia before the Awujale to pay homage, in one of Nigeria's largest Yoruba cultural events.

period.note: Falls after the third day of Eid-el-Kabir, so it moves with the Islamic calendar

NG-OG.title: Awujale of Ijebuland
NG-OG.note: The Awujale of Ijebuland is the paramount ruler of the Ijebu kingdom, seated at Ijebu-Ode.

NG-OG.title: Osugbo society
NG-OG.note: Osugbo is the Ijebu counterpart of the Ogboni fraternity, a council of elders with judicial and ritual authority that works alongside the Awujale.

NG-OG.title: Agemo festival
NG-OG.note: Agemo is a masquerade-linked festival celebrated in Ijebu and Remo towns, centred on the chameleon-linked Agemo cult.

NG-OG.title: Alake of Egbaland
NG-OG.note: The Alake of Egbaland is the paramount ruler of the Egba, seated at Abeokuta beneath Olumo Rock.

NG-OG.title: Lisabi Festival
NG-OG.note: Egba communities commemorate Lisabi, the folk hero credited with organising the Egba revolt against Oyo overlordship in the 18th century.

NG-OG.title: Gelede masquerade
NG-OG.note: Gelede honours the power of women, especially elders, through masked dance and oral performance. It is practised by Yoruba communities in Benin and Togo as well as Nigeria, and was proclaimed by UNESCO as a masterpiece of oral and intangible heritage.

period.note: Observed before the rains, roughly March to May

NG-ON.title: Sunshine State
NG-ON.note: Ondo's nickname reflects its coastal-to-forest geography and status as one of Nigeria's leading cocoa-producing states.

NG-ON.title: Early offshore oil exploration
NG-ON.note: Ondo's coastline was the site of some of Nigeria's earliest offshore oil exploration activity.

NG-ON.title: Igogo Festival
NG-ON.note: Owo's annual Igogo festival is listed by the Federal Ministry of Information among Nigeria's ancestral festivals.

period.note: Listed for September; some accounts place it into October

NG-ON.title: Ariginya Festival
NG-ON.note: Ariginya, meaning local wrestling, is one of the foremost traditional festivals of Ikare-Akoko.

NG-ON.title: Biripo
NG-ON.note: Biripo is a major traditional music of the Ilaje, Apoi and Ikale peoples, used to teach peace, unity and productivity.

NG-ON.title: Irokute Festival
NG-ON.note: Irokute is a traditional festival of Ikaleland, studied at Okitipupa.

NG-ON.title: Jolly
NG-ON.note: A cultural form reported as unique to the Ilaje people. Details still to be confirmed with local sources.

NG-ON.title: Zion
NG-ON.note: A cultural form reported as unique to the Ilaje people. Details still to be confirmed with local sources.

NG-ON.title: Asiko
NG-ON.note: A cultural form reported as unique to the Ikale people. Details still to be confirmed with local sources.

NG-ON.title: Deji of Akure, Osemawe of Ondo and Olowo of Owo
NG-ON.note: The state's three best-known royal thrones sit at Akure, Ondo and Owo, each heading an old Yoruba kingdom.

NG-OS.title: State of the Living Spring
NG-OS.note: Osun's nickname refers to the Osun River and its sacred grove, one of the last intact sacred forests in Yorubaland and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

NG-OS.title: Cradle of the Yoruba
NG-OS.note: Ile-Ife, in Osun State, is regarded in Yoruba oral tradition as the origin point of the Yoruba people and the seat of the Ooni of Ife.

NG-OS.title: Osun-Osogbo Festival
NG-OS.note: Devotees honour the river goddess Osun at the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in a festival lasting about two weeks that peaks in August.

period.note: Usually starts in the second week of August

NG-OS.title: Olojo Festival
NG-OS.note: Ile-Ife's Olojo festival, centred on the Ooni of Ife and rites at Oke Mogun, lasts about four days in October.

NG-OS.title: Ifa divination system
NG-OS.note: The Ifa divination system, with its Odu Ifa verse corpus interpreted by a Babalawo, is central to Yoruba spirituality and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2008.

NG-OS.title: Oluwo of Iwo and Timi of Ede
NG-OS.note: Iwo and Ede are historic Oyo-Yoruba towns in Osun State, ruled by the Oluwo and the Timi respectively.

NG-OY.title: Pace-Setter State
NG-OY.note: Oyo's nickname dates to the old Western Region era, reflecting a self-image as an early mover in education and infrastructure among Nigerian states.

NG-OY.title: Old Oyo Empire legacy
NG-OY.note: The state takes its name from the historic Oyo Empire, once one of the largest and most powerful West African states, with its former capital's ruins preserved within Old Oyo National Park.

NG-OY.title: Africa's first television station
NG-OY.note: Ibadan, Oyo's capital, was home to WNTV, the first television station in Africa, launched in 1959.

NG-OY.title: Sango Festival
NG-OY.note: The World Sango Festival in Oyo honours Sango, the deified third Alaafin and Yoruba god of thunder. UNESCO inscribed it in 2023, and it marks the Yoruba traditional new year.

NG-OY.title: Alaafin of Oyo
NG-OY.note: The Alaafin is the ruler of Oyo, successor to the emperors of the Oyo Empire.

NG-OY.title: Olubadan chieftaincy line
NG-OY.note: Ibadan's Olubadan is not chosen by a single royal house; chiefs rise by seniority through the civil (Otun) and military (Balogun) lines until they reach the throne.

NG-OY.title: Oke'Badan Festival
NG-OY.note: An Ibadan festival held at Oke'Badan hill, tied to the city's founding story.

NG-OY.title: Egungun ancestral masquerades
NG-OY.note: Egungun masquerades embody ancestors returning to visit the living and are among the most widespread Yoruba traditions, with strong local calendars in Oyo State towns.

period.note: Dates differ by town

NG-OY.title: Soun of Ogbomosho
NG-OY.note: The Soun is the paramount ruler of Ogbomosho.

NG-OY.title: Aare Ona Kakanfo title
NG-OY.note: The Aare Ona Kakanfo was the commander-in-chief of the Oyo Empire's army, a title revived in the modern era.

NG-OY.title: Iseyin Aso-Oke weaving
NG-OY.note: Iseyin is a leading centre of Aso-Oke, the hand-woven Yoruba cloth used for weddings and ceremonies.

NG-PL.title: Home of Peace and Tourism
NG-PL.note: Plateau's nickname reflects its cool highland climate and historical popularity as a colonial-era tourism and retreat destination.

NG-PL.title: Colonial tin-mining boom
NG-PL.note: Jos grew rapidly from the early 1900s as a British colonial tin-mining hub, drawing migrant labour from across Nigeria and shaping the state's ethnic diversity.

NG-PL.title: Nzem Berom Festival
NG-PL.note: Nzem Berom is the umbrella cultural festival of the Berom people, combining older harvest and planting rites, with music, dance and displays from across Beromland.

period.note: First week of April; sometimes March; revived in 2016 after a gap

NG-PL.title: Gbong Gwom Jos
NG-PL.note: The Gbong Gwom Jos is the paramount Berom ruler and chairs the Plateau State Council of Traditional Rulers.

NG-RI.title: Treasure Base of the Nation
NG-RI.note: Rivers' nickname reflects its central role in Nigeria's oil and gas economy, centred on Port Harcourt.

NG-RI.title: Colonial coal-export port
NG-RI.note: Port Harcourt was founded in 1912 as a railway terminus and export port for Enugu coal, before oil later became the dominant industry.

NG-RI.title: Ekine (Sekiapu) society
NG-RI.note: Ekine, known as Sekiapu, is the masquerade and performance society central to Kalabari culture.

NG-RI.title: Amanyanabo of Kalabari
NG-RI.note: The Amanyanabo is the king of the Kalabari, seated at Buguma.

NG-RI.title: Jaja of Opobo
NG-RI.note: King Jaja founded Opobo in 1870 after breaking from Bonny and was exiled by the British in 1887.

NG-RI.title: Ogoni and the Ogoni Bill of Rights
NG-RI.note: The Ogoni of Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme drew international attention through the 1990 Ogoni Bill of Rights and Ken Saro-Wiwa's activism.

NG-SO.title: Seat of the Caliphate
NG-SO.note: Sokoto's nickname reflects its status as the historic capital of the Sokoto Caliphate, founded around 1809 by Usman dan Fodio.

NG-SO.title: Sultan of Sokoto
NG-SO.note: The Sultan of Sokoto remains Nigeria's foremost traditional Islamic authority, a title with unbroken lineage back to the Caliphate's founding.

NG-SO.title: Gobir and the Sokoto jihad
NG-SO.note: The Hausa kingdom of Gobir, in the Sabon Birni area of present-day Sokoto State, was the state whose rulers Usman dan Fodio opposed before founding the caliphate.

NG-TA.title: Nature's Gift to the Nation
NG-TA.note: Taraba's nickname reflects its varied highland-to-lowland geography, including Chappal Waddi, Nigeria's highest peak.

NG-TA.title: Nigeria's highest point
NG-TA.note: Chappal Waddi, within Gashaka-Gumti National Park, rises to roughly 2,419 metres, making it Nigeria's tallest mountain.

NG-TA.title: Nwonyo International Fishing and Cultural Festival
NG-TA.note: Held at Nwonyo Lake north of Ibi, the festival is among Nigeria's oldest fishing festivals. It was revived in 2024 after a break of about 14 years.

NG-TA.title: Aku Uka of Wukari
NG-TA.note: The Aku Uka heads the Wukari Federation, successor to the Kwararafa state of the Jukun.

NG-TA.title: Mumuye wood sculpture
NG-TA.note: Mumuye figurative wood carvings are prized in African art collections.

NG-YO.title: Pride of the Sahel
NG-YO.note: Yobe's nickname reflects its location in Nigeria's semi-arid Sahel zone, bordering Niger Republic.

NG-YO.title: Mai of Fika
NG-YO.note: The Emir of Fika bears the title Mai of Fika, heading the Bolewa-centred Fika Emirate.

NG-ZA.title: Farming is Our Pride
NG-ZA.note: Zamfara's nickname reflects its agrarian economy, especially grain and cotton farming.

NG-ZA.title: First state to adopt full Sharia
NG-ZA.note: Zamfara was the first Nigerian state to formally adopt Sharia criminal law in 1999-2000, a move that spread to several other northern states.

NG-ZA.title: Historic Zamfara Kingdom
NG-ZA.note: Zamfara was an old Hausa-speaking kingdom, counted in Hausa tradition among the Banza Bakwai states.
